title: Correct conduct
core: All four name conduct judged against a standard of correctness rather than a standard of goodness — form, not virtue. Each is formal, faintly institutional, and concerned with observing the expected outward shape of behaviour: restraint, courtesy, bearing, the done thing. A person can satisfy every one of them and still be a scoundrel; a person can violate them all without committing any moral wrong. What separates them is *what the standard governs* — the occasion, the code, the body, or the relationship between rival institutions.

words.nuance: Anchored to **the occasion in progress** — the restraint this room, this ceremony, this hearing demands right now. It's what a judge orders when the gallery starts shouting; breaching it disrupts an event rather than violating a rule you could have written down in advance.

The **code itself**, abstract and portable — invocable about conduct that happened elsewhere, last year, in private. Alone in this group it also attaches to *acts rather than persons*: you can question the propriety of an appointment, a loan, a phone call, meaning "should this have been done at all?"

The only one that is **physical** — posture, bearing, how you enter a room and hold yourself in it. It's a mark on a report card, graded by an observer watching one individual; you can have impeccable deportment standing silently alone under inspection.

The only one whose parties are **institutions, not people**, and whose politeness is *unowed* — courts, chambers, sovereign states restraining each other by choice, with no authority to compel them. Its collapse means escalation and gridlock, not embarrassment.

exam_note: Comity is the trap: it looks like a generic synonym for civility, but the sentence will always supply rival institutions (senate, nations, jurisdictions) — if the parties are individuals, it's wrong.
